What changed since the parses in synthid

Source: vignettes/articles/version-comparison.Rmd
version-comparison.Rmd

synthid’s Form 990 Part VII people tables (s3://nccs-efile/dev/synthid/partvii-v3_1/people/) were parsed in October 2026 with peopleparser commit cb01547, version 0.0.0.9000, called 0.0.9 here. This page compares those parses with version 0.2.2 on a sample of names, to show what the changes since then do to real data and where the parser is still wrong.

The sample

Twenty thousand rows were drawn at random from each of the 2017 and 2024 people files, and 10,000 distinct names taken from them. Each name was parsed again with 0.2.2, with split_run_together = TRUE and classify = TRUE, and the salutation, first, middle and last name, suffix and gender compared with the stored values. The script is data-raw/compare_versions.R; every changed name is listed in data-raw/compare-v0.0.9-v0.2.2.csv. Parts are shown below as salutation | first | middle | last | suffix.

Summary

903 of the 10,000 names (9%) parse differently. The rest are unchanged.

Change Names Assessment
Gender only 485 Mostly gains: names newly coded from the 2020 census
First and last name swapped 262 Nearly all now keep the written order
Other changes 62 Mixed; most are compound-surname order and names wrong in both
Middle name no longer joined to the surname 50 Mostly better; a few names written surname first are now wrong
Title or credential taken out of the name 41 Better
Particle joined to the surname 3 Better

split_run_together() changed none of these names: about one Part VII name in 10,000 is written as one run-together word, so a sample this size holds few or none.

Gender

Change Names
Unknown to F or M 562
Switched between F and M 98
F or M to unknown 42

Most gains come from the 2020 census given-name lists, which hold about ten times as many names as the 1990 lists the old build used. The F/M switches are unisex names whose balance moved between 1990 and 2020:

Gender for these names is close to a coin toss in either census; read the gender_confidence column before relying on it.

First and last name swapped

262 names have their first and last names swapped. In 258 the new parse keeps the order the name was written in, first name first. The old build often read a two-word name as surname first when the census leaned that way at all.

Middle names that are also surnames

The old build joined a middle name to the surname whenever the census listed it more often as a surname, so DAVID LEE SMITH got the surname LEE-SMITH. Version 0.2.2 joins a middle word only when at least 90% of its census records are surnames (GARCIA LOPEZ). Initials are never joined.

Other changes

Most of the rest are compound surnames now kept in written order (GUTIERREZ-VALVERDE), stray words fixed (KENNETHVAN-DER-VLIET becomes KENNETH VAN-DER-VLIET) and DO and DOCTOR read as surnames. About half are names that are wrong in both versions: an unknown credential left in the surname (OWENS-SSND) or an organisation parsed as a person.

Name types

classify_names() labels 19 of the 10,000 entries (0.19%) as something other than a person. Nearly all are right; Sun Cheer Sheen is a person labelled an organisation, and METTA WORLD PEACE (the basketball player’s legal name) is labelled a person and an organisation.

Gaps that persist

  • An unlisted given name before a listed name. A word missing from the census counts as a likely surname, so DR MASSUMEH FARHAD, CLEVELAND TAYLER and CHIYA AYDIN AYHAN are read as written surname first.
  • Names written surname first with weak evidence. The written-order rule keeps the order unless the census is clear, so WALPERT LEVY TARA and Soh Yeun Kim are read in written order.
  • Credentials the lists do not know stay in the surname: SSND, SIOR, CNHA, MSCJ, FCAP, FACFAS, CPPO, CPSM, VG. Add them with prefixes = c(prx, ...).
  • Organisations and notes in person fields are parsed as people (NORTHWESTERN MUTUAL LIFE INSURANCE COMPANY, PHILIP JONES VISIT DALLAS). Use classify = TRUE and drop the entries that are not people.
  • Unisex names (KERRY, TAYLOR, KRIS, RILEY) get a gender close to a coin toss.
  • Double surnames made of common given names (LEE, RAY, GRANT) are now split into a middle name and a surname.
